# Large multi-feature tasks

When a request is big — multiple features, or a large ask that naturally splits into independent
pieces of work — do not implement it as one monolithic pass. Split it into separate commits, one
per feature/unit of work, and drive each unit through this graph-engineering framework using the
Agent tool:

```
Task -> Planner -> Worker -> [Reviewer 1, Reviewer 2, ... Reviewer N] -> Synthesise -> Pass?
                     ^                                                        |
                     |-------------------- feedback (no) ---------------------|
                                                                               |
                                                                          (yes) -> commit -> next unit
```

- **Planner**: breaks the overall ask into an ordered list of commit-sized units of work (a
  Plan Reviewer can review the plan itself before execution starts; route its feedback back to
  the Planner and send a summary of plan feedback to the user).
- **Worker**: a resident agent (kept alive across the reviewer round for a given unit) that
  implements one unit of work.
- **Reviewers (1..N)**: spawn multiple reviewer agents in parallel against the Worker's output —
  e.g. correctness, simplification/efficiency, and test coverage as separate reviewer passes.
  These can be ephemeral (fresh agent per round).
- **Synthesise**: reconcile the reviewers' findings into one set of required changes.
- **Pass? gate**: if synthesised feedback has no blocking issues, finalize and commit that unit
  with its own commit message, then move to the next planned unit. If it fails, send the
  synthesised feedback back to the Worker as another round on the same unit (don't restart from
  the Planner unless the feedback reveals the plan itself was wrong).

Net effect: one commit per feature/unit, each vetted by multiple reviewer passes before it lands,
rather than a single large uncommitted or unreviewed diff at the end.

## Verifying UI work: visual recreation (the main way to verify)

For any unit that changes UI, the primary verification is a **visual recreation**: render the real
components with mock data and look at a screenshot. Typecheck and unit tests are necessary but do not
count as verifying how it looks. Workers should do this before reporting, and I re-do it (or open the
image for the user) when the user asks to see it.

1. Add a **temporary** preview route (e.g. `apps/web/app/zz-preview/page.tsx`) that imports the real
   components and renders them with realistic mock props: populated, empty, capped/failed, long
   names/links. Put context around them (page background, a mock frame for panels/drawers that need a
   session or client state) but never reimplement the component itself.
2. Start the dev server in the background with dummy env vars the app needs to boot (e.g.
   `CONVEX_URL=https://dummy.convex.cloud CONVEX_DEPLOY_KEY=x NEXT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 bunx next dev -p <port>`),
   wait for "Ready", and `curl` the route for a 200.
3. Screenshot with headless Chrome, not the preview MCP tools (those time out):
   `"/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome" --headless=new --disable-gpu --hide-scrollbars --force-device-scale-factor=2 --virtual-time-budget=6000 --window-size=<w>,<h> --screenshot=/tmp/<name>.png <url>`
   Take a wide desktop shot and a narrow one. Headless Chrome enforces a minimum window width, so a
   narrow shot can come out horizontally clipped; for true 320px checks render inside a 320px-wide
   iframe or measure element widths, and say so rather than treating clipping as a bug.
4. **Read the PNG** (the Read tool shows images) and actually look at it: hierarchy, spacing, truncation,
   overflow, alignment, tap targets, copy. Report what was seen versus what was not verified
   (hover/focus states, real clipboard/share, animations, Safari-only behavior, the real page behind auth).
5. For the user, `open` the desktop screenshot (copy it to `~/Downloads/<name>.png` first) since they
   can't see tool-output images.
6. **Clean up before committing**: stop the dev server (`pkill -f "next dev -p <port>"`), delete the
   preview route, temp public files and stray `.next` artifacts, and confirm `git status` shows only
   intended changes. Never commit a preview route or mocks.

# Mandatory visual + local-server verification (every agent, every run)

Applies to any task that changes code a user can see or that the running app depends on. No unit of
work is "done" until both of these have happened and been reported:

1. **Run it against the local server.** Start the real dev server (and `npx convex dev` when Convex
   code changed) in this worktree, wait for "Ready", and exercise the changed path end to end: `curl`
   the route for the expected status and hit changed API routes. A passing typecheck/lint/build alone
   does not count.
2. **Verify visually with a screenshot.** Follow the visual-recreation steps above (headless Chrome,
   wide + narrow shot), then Read the PNG and look at it. For pages behind auth, use a temporary
   preview route with mock data. Non-UI changes still get a screenshot of the affected page to prove
   nothing regressed.
3. **Report** what was seen, what was not verified (hover/focus, auth-gated pages, animations), and
   the screenshot path. If the server can't boot (e.g. missing env vars), say so explicitly and fix
   the env first (see below); never claim success without having run it.
4. Clean up (stop the server, delete preview routes/temp files) before committing.

Env vars: each worktree needs its own copy of the gitignored `.env*` files. If `.env.local` is
missing in the current worktree, symlink it from the canonical copy at `~/.config/avian/.env.local`
(`ln -s ~/.config/avian/.env.local .env.local`) before starting the server.

1	# AgentBisect — neatHack Plan
2	
3	Oct 8, 2026 · @Jaxson
4	
5	## The idea
6	
7	AgentBisect is `git bisect` for agent behavior. Hand it one bad neatlogs trace and it finds the commit that caused the regression, explains why that commit was written, and ships a verified fix.
8	
9	### The problem
10	
11	- Agents regress silently. A prompt tweak, a new tool or a model swap makes the agent pick the wrong tool, loop, or burn tokens, and nothing crashes.
12	- `git bisect` can't help. It needs a reliable pass/fail test, and agent behavior is probabilistic.
13	- Teams eyeball traces and guess. With coding agents writing most commits, nobody remembers why a given change was made.
14	
15	### What AgentBisect does
16	
17	1. **Intake.** You point it at a failing trace or detection in neatlogs, or at a GitHub issue describing the bad behavior. It pulls the failing trace plus passing traces from before, and turns them into an eval suite, a held-out set, and a pass/fail rule.
18	2. **Smart bisect.** It finds where the good and bad traces diverge, uses entire-graph to find the code tied to that point, and ranks the commits that touched it by what their Entire checkpoints say they were for. It tests the likeliest commits first in isolated worktrees, and falls back to plain bisect if they come back clean. Every run is traced in neatlogs and tagged with its commit; flaky results get extra repeats, and commits that don't build are skipped.
19	3. **Explain.** At the culprit commit it reads the Entire checkpoint: the prompt and reasoning of the coding agent that wrote the change. It adds entire-graph's semantic diff and blast radius, and diffs the good and bad traces span by span to find where behavior diverged.
20	4. **Fix.** A coding agent writes a fix that keeps the change's original intent and removes only the regression.
21	5. **Verify.** A revert test proves the culprit: revert it on HEAD and the regression must disappear. The fix must then match the good commit's score on the full suite, including held-out cases the fixer never saw, and still pass a test for the original intent; otherwise it loops back to Fix.
22	6. **Report.** It opens a PR with the culprit, the original intent, the fix, and before/after trace links with numbers.
23	7. **Watch mode.** It polls neatlogs detection trends and starts an investigation on its own when one spikes, so nobody has to notice the regression first.
24	
25	### Why it wins neatHack
26	
27	| Judging category | Weight | How AgentBisect scores |
28	| --- | --- | --- |
29	| The agent | 30% | A long multi-step task that hits every focus area: planning (the bisect plan), state across dozens of runs, recovery (flaky results, broken commits, resume after a crash), verification and iteration |
30	| Use of neatlogs + Entire | 25% | Both are runtime inputs, not decoration: neatlogs is the oracle, Entire checkpoints are the evidence of intent. Remove either and the agent can't work |
31	| Demo video | 20% | A clear visual story: bad trace, bisect narrowing on screen, the culprit's original prompt, fix, green before/after traces |
32	| Building in public | 15% | Every stage produces a shareable clip or trace screenshot |
33	| Usefulness + originality | 10% | Every team shipping agents hits this. It extends neatlogs Fixes with what Fixes lacks: finding the commit and proving the fix |
34	
35	The evidence the judges ask for falls out of normal runs: before/after traces with numbers, a failure-recovery run, and Entire checkpoints.
36	
37	### Focus-area coverage
38	
39	| Focus area | Where AgentBisect shows it |
40	| --- | --- |
41	| Planning | Smart bisect plans which commits to test from trace divergence, code impact and checkpoint intent |
42	| Tool use | git worktrees, neatlogs MCP, Entire CLI, entire-graph, eval runner and `gh`, each picked from the evidence at hand |
43	| State | State file after every step; per-commit verdicts reused by later investigations on the same repo |
44	| Context | entire-graph narrows what gets read; context tokens per step are logged in neatlogs, with and without the graph |
45	| Execution | Dozens of eval runs over 30–60+ minutes, unattended |
46	| Recovery | Skips broken commits, adds repeats for flaky results, survives rate limits and timeouts, resumes after a kill, retries failed fixes |
47	| Verification | The revert test proves the culprit; held-out evals and the intent test prove the fix |
48	| Iteration | Each verdict re-ranks the remaining commits; each failed fix feeds the next attempt |
49	
50	It also maps onto two of the page's example tasks: "Fix a GitHub issue" (issue in, tested PR out) and "Watch a running system" (watch mode).
51	
52	### Scope for the hackathon
53	
54	- **In:** one realistic demo target agent whose 15–25 commit history contains three regressions as plausible side effects of real features; a Python CLI; trace, detection or GitHub-issue intake; watch mode; a Markdown/HTML report; a GitHub PR.
55	- **Out (next steps in the pitch):** multi-repo support, a hosted web app, parallel fixer agents, re-planning when new commits land mid-investigation.
56	
57	## Architecture
58	
59	Two public repos, one Python CLI, six stages. neatlogs supplies the pass/fail signal at every commit; Entire supplies the reason each change exists.
60	
61	[embedded content: AgentBisect pipeline · 6 stages, 1 retry loop\]
62	
63	The top row finds and explains the culprit; the bottom row fixes it, proves the fix, and reports.
64	
65	### Components
66	
67	| Component | What it does | Built with |
68	| --- | --- | --- |
69	| Target agent (demo victim) | A realistic tool-using agent, e.g. a support agent with search, lookup and refund tools. Its repo history holds three regressions that arrived as side effects of real features | Python, Claude via Bedrock or the Anthropic API, neatlogs SDK |
70	| Eval harness | Runs one eval case against the target agent at a given commit; returns pass/fail and the trace id | Deterministic checks first (tool chosen, output schema), then an LLM judge rubric |
71	| Intake (`intake.py`) | Turns a bad trace, a detection or a GitHub issue into a RegressionSpec with an eval suite and a held-out set | neatlogs MCP: `search_traces`, `get_trace_context`, `list_detections`; `gh` for issues |
72	| Watcher (`watch.py`) | Polls detection trends and starts an investigation when one spikes | neatlogs MCP: `get_detection_trend` |
73	| Planner (`planner.py`) | Smart bisect: ranks candidate commits from trace divergence, code impact and checkpoint intent; falls back to plain bisect | Span diff of traces, `entire graph impact`, Entire checkpoints |
74	| Bisect engine (`bisect.py`) | Runs the planner's order: decides good / bad / skip, handles flaky results, re-ranks after every verdict | git worktrees, repeated runs with a confidence band |
75	| Culprit analyst (`culprit.py`) | Explains the culprit commit | The commit's Entire checkpoint (prompt + reasoning), `entire graph diff` and `entire graph impact` |
76	| Fixer (`fixer.py`) | Writes the fix in a worktree | Claude Agent SDK or Claude Code headless, with Entire on so the fix is itself a checkpoint |
77	| Verifier (`verify.py`) | Proves the culprit (revert test) and the fix (full suite incl. held-out cases, plus intent test) | Same eval harness, compared with the good-commit baseline |
78	| Reporter (`report.py`) | Opens the PR and writes the report, including a confidence level and a warning when results suggest more than one regression | `gh` CLI, links to neatlogs traces and Entire checkpoints |
79	| State store (`state.py`) | Saves progress after every step; keeps per-commit verdicts for reuse | JSON file in `.agentbisect/` |
80	
81	### How each sponsor is used
82	
83	| Tool | Role in the running agent | Role in how you build it |
84	| --- | --- | --- |
85	| neatlogs | The oracle: every eval run is traced and tagged (commit, bisect run, case). Intake and watch mode read traces and detections through MCP. AgentBisect's own run is traced, including context tokens per step. Its prompts live in neatlogs prompt versions behind a `production` label | Instrumented from the first commit; you use its traces to find and fix AgentBisect's own bugs, which gives the before/after evidence |
86	| Entire | Checkpoint intent ranks candidate commits and explains the culprit; entire-graph ties the trace divergence to code, narrows context, and gives the semantic diff; fix commits become new checkpoints | On for the whole build in both repos. The target repo's history is written by a coding agent, so its checkpoints are real |
87	| cfo.ai | None | Prices AgentBisect as a product: cost per investigation, pricing, margin, runway |
88	| AWS Bedrock (optional) | Model calls for the target agent and evals, paid with hackathon credits | None |
89	
90	Two measured claims come straight from these roles: smart bisect needs fewer eval rounds than plain bisect, and entire-graph cuts context tokens per step. Both numbers are read off neatlogs traces.
91	
92	### The smart bisect loop
93	
94	1. **Resolve the range.** Good = newest commit whose tagged traces pass; bad = the failing trace's commit (or HEAD). Re-run both ends once to confirm they really are good and bad.
95	2. **Find the divergence.** Diff the good and bad traces span by span to find the first step where behavior differs (e.g. picked `refund_order` instead of `lookup_order`).
96	3. **Rank candidates.** Use `entire graph impact` to find code tied to that step, keep the commits in range that touch it, and order them by how well their Entire checkpoint intent matches the symptom.
97	4. **Test the top candidate and its parent** in fresh worktrees: K cases × R repeats in parallel (start at K = 8, R = 3), every run tagged with commit, investigation id and case. Install or import failure → skip and take the next candidate. Inside the uncertainty band → add repeats (up to a cap).
98	5. **Re-rank after each verdict.** A clean top candidate drops out and the next is tested. If every ranked candidate is clean, fall back to plain bisect over the whole range (about log2 N steps; 5 for 20 commits).
99	6. **Save state after every step** until one commit is confirmed, then hand it to the revert test in Verify.
100	
101	Plain bisect stays in the code as the baseline: run both on the same regression and report eval rounds and cost for each.
102	
103	### Key data shapes
104	
105	```python
106	RegressionSpec: source (trace | detection | issue), bad_trace_id, good_trace_ids,
107	                cases[], held_out[], predicate (checks + rubric), metric
108	Plan:           divergent_span, impacted_symbols, candidates[{sha, score, reason}], mode (smart | plain)
109	BisectState:    good_sha, bad_sha, plan, results{sha: verdict, pass_rate, trace_ids}, step, status,
110	                context_tokens_per_step[]
111	CulpritReport:  sha, checkpoint_intent, semantic_diff, impacted_symbols, revert_test_passed, confidence
112	FixAttempt:     branch, diff, eval_score, held_out_score, intent_test_passed, trace_ids, attempt
113	```
114	
115	### Repo layout
116	
117	```
118	agentbisect/                 # the agent (public, Entire on)
119	  agentbisect/
120	    cli.py  intake.py  bisect.py  runner.py  judge.py
121	    culprit.py  fixer.py  verify.py  report.py  state.py
122	    prompts/                 # mirrored from neatlogs prompt versions

134	- The exact Entire CLI command to read a commit's checkpoint session ([CLI reference](https://docs.entire.io/cli-reference)).
135	- Whether neatlogs tags can be filtered through MCP `search_traces`, or need the [Public API](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference).

138	## Demo target agent: tools and eval cases
139	
140	The target is a customer-support agent for a small online store: five mocked tools, 24 eval cases, and three planted regressions that each break a known set of cases.
141	
142	### Tools
143	
144	All tools are mocked over fixed seed data in `data/` (about 12 orders: processing, shipped, delivered, delivered over 30 days ago, already refunded, and one $800 order), so every run is repeatable.

# AgentBisect — neatHack Plan

Oct 8, 2026 · @Jaxson

## The idea

AgentBisect is `git bisect` for agent behavior. Hand it one bad neatlogs trace and it finds the commit that caused the regression, explains why that commit was written, and ships a verified fix.

### The problem

- Agents regress silently. A prompt tweak, a new tool or a model swap makes the agent pick the wrong tool, loop, or burn tokens, and nothing crashes.
- `git bisect` can't help. It needs a reliable pass/fail test, and agent behavior is probabilistic.
- Teams eyeball traces and guess. With coding agents writing most commits, nobody remembers why a given change was made.

### What AgentBisect does

1. **Intake.** You point it at a failing trace or detection in neatlogs, or at a GitHub issue describing the bad behavior. It pulls the failing trace plus passing traces from before, and turns them into an eval suite, a held-out set, and a pass/fail rule.
2. **Smart bisect.** It finds where the good and bad traces diverge, uses entire-graph to find the code tied to that point, and ranks the commits that touched it by what their Entire checkpoints say they were for. It tests the likeliest commits first in isolated worktrees, and falls back to plain bisect if they come back clean. Every run is traced in neatlogs and tagged with its commit; flaky results get extra repeats, and commits that don't build are skipped.
3. **Explain.** At the culprit commit it reads the Entire checkpoint: the prompt and reasoning of the coding agent that wrote the change. It adds entire-graph's semantic diff and blast radius, and diffs the good and bad traces span by span to find where behavior diverged.
4. **Fix.** A coding agent writes a fix that keeps the change's original intent and removes only the regression.
5. **Verify.** A revert test proves the culprit: revert it on HEAD and the regression must disappear. The fix must then match the good commit's score on the full suite, including held-out cases the fixer never saw, and still pass a test for the original intent; otherwise it loops back to Fix.
6. **Report.** It opens a PR with the culprit, the original intent, the fix, and before/after trace links with numbers.
7. **Watch mode.** It polls neatlogs detection trends and starts an investigation on its own when one spikes, so nobody has to notice the regression first.

### Why it wins neatHack

| Judging category | Weight | How AgentBisect scores |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The agent | 30% | A long multi-step task that hits every focus area: planning (the bisect plan), state across dozens of runs, recovery (flaky results, broken commits, resume after a crash), verification and iteration |
| Use of neatlogs + Entire | 25% | Both are runtime inputs, not decoration: neatlogs is the oracle, Entire checkpoints are the evidence of intent. Remove either and the agent can't work |
| Demo video | 20% | A clear visual story: bad trace, bisect narrowing on screen, the culprit's original prompt, fix, green before/after traces |
| Building in public | 15% | Every stage produces a shareable clip or trace screenshot |
| Usefulness + originality | 10% | Every team shipping agents hits this. It extends neatlogs Fixes with what Fixes lacks: finding the commit and proving the fix |

The evidence the judges ask for falls out of normal runs: before/after traces with numbers, a failure-recovery run, and Entire checkpoints.

### Focus-area coverage

| Focus area | Where AgentBisect shows it |
| --- | --- |
| Planning | Smart bisect plans which commits to test from trace divergence, code impact and checkpoint intent |
| Tool use | git worktrees, neatlogs MCP, Entire CLI, entire-graph, eval runner and `gh`, each picked from the evidence at hand |
| State | State file after every step; per-commit verdicts reused by later investigations on the same repo |
| Context | entire-graph narrows what gets read; context tokens per step are logged in neatlogs, with and without the graph |
| Execution | Dozens of eval runs over 30–60+ minutes, unattended |
| Recovery | Skips broken commits, adds repeats for flaky results, survives rate limits and timeouts, resumes after a kill, retries failed fixes |
| Verification | The revert test proves the culprit; held-out evals and the intent test prove the fix |
| Iteration | Each verdict re-ranks the remaining commits; each failed fix feeds the next attempt |

It also maps onto two of the page's example tasks: "Fix a GitHub issue" (issue in, tested PR out) and "Watch a running system" (watch mode).

### Scope for the hackathon

- **In:** one realistic demo target agent whose 15–25 commit history contains three regressions as plausible side effects of real features; a Python CLI; trace, detection or GitHub-issue intake; watch mode; a Markdown/HTML report; a GitHub PR.
- **Out (next steps in the pitch):** multi-repo support, a hosted web app, parallel fixer agents, re-planning when new commits land mid-investigation.

## Architecture

Two public repos, one Python CLI, six stages. neatlogs supplies the pass/fail signal at every commit; Entire supplies the reason each change exists.

[embedded content: AgentBisect pipeline · 6 stages, 1 retry loop\]

The top row finds and explains the culprit; the bottom row fixes it, proves the fix, and reports.

### Components

| Component | What it does | Built with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target agent (demo victim) | A realistic tool-using agent, e.g. a support agent with search, lookup and refund tools. Its repo history holds three regressions that arrived as side effects of real features | Python, Claude via Bedrock or the Anthropic API, neatlogs SDK |
| Eval harness | Runs one eval case against the target agent at a given commit; returns pass/fail and the trace id | Deterministic checks first (tool chosen, output schema), then an LLM judge rubric |
| Intake (`intake.py`) | Turns a bad trace, a detection or a GitHub issue into a RegressionSpec with an eval suite and a held-out set | neatlogs MCP: `search_traces`, `get_trace_context`, `list_detections`; `gh` for issues |
| Watcher (`watch.py`) | Polls detection trends and starts an investigation when one spikes | neatlogs MCP: `get_detection_trend` |
| Planner (`planner.py`) | Smart bisect: ranks candidate commits from trace divergence, code impact and checkpoint intent; falls back to plain bisect | Span diff of traces, `entire graph impact`, Entire checkpoints |
| Bisect engine (`bisect.py`) | Runs the planner's order: decides good / bad / skip, handles flaky results, re-ranks after every verdict | git worktrees, repeated runs with a confidence band |
| Culprit analyst (`culprit.py`) | Explains the culprit commit | The commit's Entire checkpoint (prompt + reasoning), `entire graph diff` and `entire graph impact` |
| Fixer (`fixer.py`) | Writes the fix in a worktree | Claude Agent SDK or Claude Code headless, with Entire on so the fix is itself a checkpoint |
| Verifier (`verify.py`) | Proves the culprit (revert test) and the fix (full suite incl. held-out cases, plus intent test) | Same eval harness, compared with the good-commit baseline |
| Reporter (`report.py`) | Opens the PR and writes the report, including a confidence level and a warning when results suggest more than one regression | `gh` CLI, links to neatlogs traces and Entire checkpoints |
| State store (`state.py`) | Saves progress after every step; keeps per-commit verdicts for reuse | JSON file in `.agentbisect/` |

### How each sponsor is used

| Tool | Role in the running agent | Role in how you build it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| neatlogs | The oracle: every eval run is traced and tagged (commit, bisect run, case). Intake and watch mode read traces and detections through MCP. AgentBisect's own run is traced, including context tokens per step. Its prompts live in neatlogs prompt versions behind a `production` label | Instrumented from the first commit; you use its traces to find and fix AgentBisect's own bugs, which gives the before/after evidence |
| Entire | Checkpoint intent ranks candidate commits and explains the culprit; entire-graph ties the trace divergence to code, narrows context, and gives the semantic diff; fix commits become new checkpoints | On for the whole build in both repos. The target repo's history is written by a coding agent, so its checkpoints are real |
| cfo.ai | None | Prices AgentBisect as a product: cost per investigation, pricing, margin, runway |
| AWS Bedrock (optional) | Model calls for the target agent and evals, paid with hackathon credits | None |

Two measured claims come straight from these roles: smart bisect needs fewer eval rounds than plain bisect, and entire-graph cuts context tokens per step. Both numbers are read off neatlogs traces.

### The smart bisect loop

1. **Resolve the range.** Good = newest commit whose tagged traces pass; bad = the failing trace's commit (or HEAD). Re-run both ends once to confirm they really are good and bad.
2. **Find the divergence.** Diff the good and bad traces span by span to find the first step where behavior differs (e.g. picked `refund_order` instead of `lookup_order`).
3. **Rank candidates.** Use `entire graph impact` to find code tied to that step, keep the commits in range that touch it, and order them by how well their Entire checkpoint intent matches the symptom.
4. **Test the top candidate and its parent** in fresh worktrees: K cases × R repeats in parallel (start at K = 8, R = 3), every run tagged with commit, investigation id and case. Install or import failure → skip and take the next candidate. Inside the uncertainty band → add repeats (up to a cap).
5. **Re-rank after each verdict.** A clean top candidate drops out and the next is tested. If every ranked candidate is clean, fall back to plain bisect over the whole range (about log2 N steps; 5 for 20 commits).
6. **Save state after every step** until one commit is confirmed, then hand it to the revert test in Verify.

Plain bisect stays in the code as the baseline: run both on the same regression and report eval rounds and cost for each.

### Key data shapes

```python
RegressionSpec: source (trace | detection | issue), bad_trace_id, good_trace_ids,
                cases[], held_out[], predicate (checks + rubric), metric
Plan:           divergent_span, impacted_symbols, candidates[{sha, score, reason}], mode (smart | plain)
BisectState:    good_sha, bad_sha, plan, results{sha: verdict, pass_rate, trace_ids}, step, status,
                context_tokens_per_step[]
CulpritReport:  sha, checkpoint_intent, semantic_diff, impacted_symbols, revert_test_passed, confidence
FixAttempt:     branch, diff, eval_score, held_out_score, intent_test_passed, trace_ids, attempt
```

### Repo layout

```
agentbisect/                 # the agent (public, Entire on)
  agentbisect/
    cli.py  intake.py  bisect.py  runner.py  judge.py
    culprit.py  fixer.py  verify.py  report.py  state.py
    prompts/                 # mirrored from neatlogs prompt versions
  evidence/                  # trace links, screenshots, checkpoint exports
  hackathon.md               # build log from the neatHack skill
  README.md

support-agent-demo/          # target agent with planted regressions (public, Entire on)
  agent/  tools/
  evals/cases.jsonl
```

### Open questions to settle in the first hour on Saturday

- The exact Entire CLI command to read a commit's checkpoint session ([CLI reference](https://docs.entire.io/cli-reference)).
- Whether neatlogs tags can be filtered through MCP `search_traces`, or need the [Public API](https://docs.neatlogs.com/api-reference).
- Whether Bedrock credits arrive in time; otherwise use the Anthropic API.

## Demo target agent: tools and eval cases

The target is a customer-support agent for a small online store: five mocked tools, 24 eval cases, and three planted regressions that each break a known set of cases.

### Tools

All tools are mocked over fixed seed data in `data/` (about 12 orders: processing, shipped, delivered, delivered over 30 days ago, already refunded, and one $800 order), so every run is repeatable.

| Tool | Inputs | Returns | Rules in the system prompt |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `lookup_order` | order id or email | status, items, amount (USD), ship date, tracking number | Always look up the order before any action |
| `search_help` | query | top 3 help-center articles (returns, shipping times, warranty) | Use for policy questions; quote the policy |
| `issue_refund` | order id, amount, reason | refund id, amount | Only within 30 days of delivery and up to the order total |
| `escalate_to_human` | summary, priority | ticket id | Angry customers, policy exceptions, anything over $500 |
| `cancel_order` | order id | confirmation | Added in R1's commit; only for orders not yet shipped |

### Eval cases

24 cases: 18 in the main suite and 6 held out (one per category, except multi-step). Every case also has a budget check: steps ≤ 6 and tokens ≤ 1.5× the good commit's median, set from the ground-truth run.

| Category | Cases | Example input | Pass check (deterministic) | Broken by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Order status | 5 | "Where is order 1042?" | Calls `lookup_order` only; reply has the tracking number; no write tool called | R1 |
| Refund within policy | 4 | "Order 1007 arrived broken, I want my money back" | `issue_refund` with the order total; reply states the right dollar amount | R3 |
| Refund outside policy | 3 | "Refund order 0991" (delivered 45 days ago) | No `issue_refund`; explains the policy or escalates | None (control) |
| Cancel requests | 3 | "Cancel 1050, I ordered by mistake" (not shipped) | `cancel_order` once; for a shipped order, no cancel and a return offered instead | None; intent test for R1's fix |
| Policy questions | 4 | "What's your return window?" | `search_help` called; answer says 30 days | R2 (budget) |
| Escalation | 3 | "Third time asking, I want a manager" or an $800 refund | `escalate_to_human` called; no refund issued | R2 (budget) |
| Multi-step | 2 | "Is 1042 shipped? If not, cancel it" | Correct branch taken for the order's real status | R1 |

### Planted regressions

| # | Feature asked of the coding agent | Side effect | Cases that fail |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| R1 (around commit 6) | Add `cancel_order`, described as "use for any order question" | Status questions trigger a cancel instead of a lookup | Order status, multi-step |
| R2 (around commit 11) | "Make the agent more thorough: always verify with search, retry when unsure" + a higher step limit | Same answers at about 3× the tokens, sometimes looping | Budget checks on every case, worst on policy and escalation |
| R3 (around commit 16) | "Return amounts in cents, to match Stripe" | Prompt and replies still assume dollars, so $12 becomes $1,200 | Refund within policy |

The controls and cancel cases keep passing throughout, which proves AgentBisect isolates the right failures. They also give each fix an intent test: R1's fix must keep cancellations working, and R3's fix must keep cents internally while showing dollars to the customer. Say in the README and video that the regressions were seeded.

## Evidence, demo and risks

Every proof the judges ask for comes out of a normal AgentBisect run, so collect it into `evidence/` as you go rather than at the end.

### Evidence checklist

- [ ] Before/after on the target agent: neatlogs traces at the culprit vs after the fix, with pass rate, tokens and cost
- [ ] Smart vs plain bisect on the same regression: eval rounds and cost for each
- [ ] Revert test result proving the culprit, plus held-out scores for the fix
- [ ] Context tokens per step with and without entire-graph
- [ ] Before/after on AgentBisect itself: a bug or waste found through its own traces, fixed, re-run
- [ ] Failure recovery: a skipped broken commit, a natural failure (rate limit or timeout), and a killed-then-resumed run
- [ ] Watch mode: a detection spike that started an investigation with no human prompt
- [ ] Entire checkpoints from both repos, plus entire-graph diff and impact output for a culprit
- [ ] Links to every #neatHack post
- [ ] Public repos with all commits dated Oct 10–12
- [ ] cfo.ai model link or screenshot

### Demo video (under 3:00)

| Time | What's on screen |
| --- | --- |
| 0:00–0:20 | Hook: a detection spikes in neatlogs and AgentBisect starts on its own. "18 commits. Which one?" |
| 0:20–0:45 | The architecture diagram; name both tools and their roles |
| 0:45–1:25 | Smart bisect: trace divergence → entire-graph impact → ranked commits; runs streaming into neatlogs tagged by commit; a broken commit skipped |
| 1:25–1:50 | Culprit: its Entire checkpoint shows the original prompt; revert test confirms it |
| 1:50–2:25 | Fix and verify: held-out scores, before/after traces with numbers; the PR opened |
| 2:25–2:40 | The numbers: smart vs plain bisect rounds, context tokens with vs without entire-graph |
| 2:40–2:58 | cfo.ai economics; recap per tool of architecture, implementation, runtime, reasoning and result |

The rules require the video to cover both neatlogs and Entire across those five aspects, so the recap is not optional.

### Risks and fallbacks

| Risk | Fallback |
| --- | --- |
| Judges see "just git bisect" | Lead the demo with smart bisect and its measured win over plain bisect |
| Demo looks staged | Regressions are side effects of real features written by a coding agent; show one full real run with timestamps; capture natural failures too |
| LLM noise makes good/bad calls unreliable | Deterministic checks first, temperature 0, extra repeats inside the confidence band |
| Two overlapping regressions mislead the search | Report a confidence level and flag "multiple regressions likely" when verdicts conflict; the revert test catches a wrong culprit |
| Fix overfits the eval suite | Held-out cases the fixer never sees; intent test |
| Eval runs too slow or costly to show live | Cache results per (commit, case) for re-takes only; small model for the target agent |
| Reading Entire checkpoints is harder than expected | Fall back to entire.io session pages plus commit metadata; entire-graph still runs locally |
| Repos without Entire checkpoints (judge question) | Rank by commit messages and PR descriptions instead; it works, with less insight into intent, which is the case for Entire |
| neatlogs MCP can't filter by tag | Use the Public API, or keep trace ids from each run in the state file |
| Seen as competing with neatlogs Fixes | Pitch it as upstream of Fixes: Fixes suggests what to change; AgentBisect finds which commit and proves the fix |
| Fixer can't produce a passing fix | Max 3 attempts; then open a draft PR with culprit, intent and the closest attempt |
| Running out of time | MVP = intake, smart bisect, culprit, revert test, report. Then fix and verify; then watch mode, recovery and dogfooding |

(There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

# Trace an AI agent with Neatlogs

Set up Neatlogs tracing in this working directory. Follow these steps in order.

## Step 1: Set up Neatlogs access

Neatlogs project ID: `110108af-1737-47ee-8494-cf482d13defd`

Set `NEATLOGS_API_KEY` to the key below in the shell the user will run the app from,
for example `export NEATLOGS_API_KEY="REDACTED"`. If the app loads a
`.env` file, add it there instead. Do not commit the key to version control.

```
REDACTED
```

Never replace this key with a guessed or invented one. This is an SDK project key, not a public API CLI credential. SDK Doctor verification can use it without CLI login. CLI readback requires browser/device approval or a service-account token; if neither is available, mark that step "waiting on a human" and continue SDK verification.

The CLI host is the dashboard origin `https://app.neatlogs.com`, not the ingest endpoint. Use this host explicitly on every CLI command.

## Step 2: Detect the language and stack

Look at the workspace and determine the language and which LLM providers / agent frameworks it uses. If the project spans more than one language, instrument each one. If the project is a monorepo, check the git root to get oriented, but only ever instrument services in or below the current working directory — never a sibling or parent app outside it, even if a workspace/compose config references one.

**Finding independent services.** A monorepo can bundle several independently-deployable services; each one that reaches an LLM/agent/tool call gets treated as its own entry point later (own workflow name in Step 4) — skip health/readiness/CRUD-only services that never call a model entirely. Check these signals in order and stop at the first one that finds more than one service directory:

1. **Workspace config** (most authoritative) — a `workspaces` field in the root `package.json`, or a `packages` field in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`. Resolve those glob patterns to directories, then keep only the ones that actually have their own manifest (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, etc.) — a glob can match a plain non-package directory too.
2. **docker-compose** — `docker-compose.yml`/`docker-compose.yaml`/`compose.yml`/`compose.yaml` at the root. Each entry under `services:` whose `build` (a plain string, or an object's `context` field) resolves to an existing directory is one service.
3. **Scattered manifests** (fallback, only if neither signal above found more than one) — search for manifest files (`package.json`, `pyproject.toml`, `go.mod`, etc.) up to 4 directories deep, excluding `node_modules`, `.git`, `dist`, `build`, `.next`, `venv`, `.venv`, **`pycache`**, `target`, `.turbo`, `vendor`. Drop the repo root's own manifest (that's the whole-repo language, not a separate service) and drop any candidate directory that's nested inside another candidate — a service's own internal shared-lib subpackage is not a separate service.

Edge case: if exactly one of these signals finds exactly one nested service, and the repo root itself has no manifest/language of its own, use that single nested directory as the actual service root instead of the top-level directory — it IS the real service, just not living at the repo root (e.g. a `services/api/` with nothing else at the top level).

If none of the three signals finds more than one candidate, treat the whole repo at the current working directory as a single service — this is the common case, and nothing else here changes for it. For every service found this way, only keep it if it reaches an LLM/agent/tool call — drop the rest, per the CRUD/health-check exclusion above.

**Identifying entry points within each service.** A single service usually has several independent, separately-triggerable capabilities — these are the actual entry points, not the service as a whole. Typical shapes: an HTTP route, a CLI command/subcommand, a cron/scheduled job, a queue/stream consumer (Kafka/SQS/Celery/RabbitMQ/BullMQ — one entry point per message/task type, not one for the whole consumer loop), a webhook/event handler, an agent-loop iteration, or a public library API function. Two things commonly get this wrong:

- **Altitude** — an internal helper the entry point calls into (`run_pipeline`, `process_document`, `process_chunk`) is NOT itself an entry point; the entry point is the outer route/command/job that calls it.
- **Multiplexed entry** — if one transport dispatches to several different capabilities (a single `/run` route branching on a `task_type` field, a Celery task branching by job kind, an argparse dispatcher, a Kafka consumer loop branching on `msg.topic`/`event_type`), treat EACH BRANCH as its own entry point — never the shared dispatcher as one entry point covering all of them.

For each entry point, also note its process kind — it changes how you initialize and where spans root:

- **One-shot script**: initialize once near the top, and end by flushing/shutting down the SDK (its process exits immediately after, and unflushed spans batched in memory are otherwise lost).
- **Long-running server**: initialize once at process startup — never inside a request handler — and only flush/shut down on process shutdown, not per request. Root each request under its own span (e.g. a `WORKFLOW` on the handler) so concurrent requests don't share one trace.
- **Concurrent operations within one entry point** (goroutines, worker threads, manual thread pools — not plain `async`/`await` in the same coroutine, which propagates context on its own): context does not always propagate automatically across a new thread or goroutine. Check Step 3's reference for whether this language/runtime requires threading the trace context through explicitly (Go always does) or handles it for you.

Neatlogs has a native SDK for Python, TypeScript, and Go — if the detected language is one of those, continue to Step 3. For any OTHER language, there is no Neatlogs SDK; pick ONE of these two paths instead, and skip Step 3 (its SDK integration-mechanism guidance is not applicable here):

- **Default: the dependency-free HTTP endpoint.** Use this unless the app already has OpenTelemetry, or the language's OTel support is clearly the more idiomatic fit (e.g. Java, .NET). Follow https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/http-injection exactly, but send to the regional URL `https://ingest.neatlogs.com/v1/trace` instead of any default host shown in the guide. The mechanism is fundamentally different from Steps 3–4 below: build ONE nested JSON tree (an object with a `children` array) as the code for one entry-point invocation runs, then send it as a SINGLE `POST /v1/trace` when that invocation completes — success or error, so wrap the send in this language's try/finally-equivalent. Never POST once per span; that violates the endpoint's contract and produces disconnected traces instead of one.
- **OpenTelemetry / OTLP-gRPC, when the app already emits OpenTelemetry spans** (its own `tracer.start_span()`-style setup, an OTel Collector, or a GenAI-instrumented framework) **or you're setting one up now:** if there's no existing OTel SDK for this language yet, find and install the official one from https://opentelemetry.io/docs/languages/ (its own site — Neatlogs doesn't ship or document per-language OTel setup beyond Python/TS/Go) and add a standard gRPC trace exporter. Either way, point the exporter at Neatlogs: endpoint `ingest.neatlogs.com:443`, gRPC protocol, and the project key sent as the `x-api-key` gRPC metadata key — NOT an `Authorization: Bearer` header. Standard: emit spans following the official OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions (https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) — `gen_ai.system`, `gen_ai.request.model`, `gen_ai.operation.name`, token/usage attributes, etc. (If this happens to be a TypeScript app already using the Vercel AI SDK's own built-in `experimental_telemetry` rather than the Neatlogs SDK, its native `ai.*` attribute format — `ai.prompt`, `ai.response.text`, `ai.operationId`, etc. — is also recognized directly; no need to convert it to `gen_ai.*`.) Spans that don't follow either of these two shapes still get ingested, but arrive as generic, unparsed spans — no model name, no token counts, no LLM-specific rendering in the dashboard. Full transport detail (including the "flush before the process exits or batched spans are silently dropped" footgun): https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/opentelemetry.

## Step 3: Follow the SDK's instrumentation reference

Python, TypeScript, or Go only — skip this step if you took one of the two paths above instead.

For each language, read the matching page and follow it exactly for HOW to capture LLM/framework calls — it lists, per provider and per framework, whether that one needs `wrap()`, `instrumentations=[...]`, or a dedicated integration helper, and that list changes as the SDK evolves, so don't guess or reuse a pattern from a different provider.

| Language | Guide |
| --- | ------|
| Python | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/python |
| TypeScript | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript |
| Go | https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/go |

Use the regional Neatlogs ingest endpoint `https://ingest.neatlogs.com` for SDK initialization. Follow the language guide for the exact endpoint parameter.

## Step 4: Install and initialize the SDK

Python, TypeScript, or Go only — if you took the OpenTelemetry or HTTP-injection path in Step 2, follow that page's own setup instructions instead of this step.

- Install the SDK using this language's own package manager (`pip`/`poetry` for Python, `npm`/`pnpm`/`yarn` for TypeScript, `go get` for Go — see Step 3's reference for the exact package/module name). Look up and install the latest version rather than pinning to a specific one. Verify the install succeeded.
- Initialize the SDK once, near the app's entry point — the exact call signature (parameter names, casing, whether the API key is passed explicitly or read from the environment automatically) differs by language, so use Step 3's reference for the precise syntax rather than guessing from another language's example. Whatever the signature, never hardcode the API key. Set the workflow name to describe the specific task or pipeline this process runs — e.g. `invoice-ocr`, `support-agent`, `checkout-flow` — not the repo or app name; the project (selected by the API key) already identifies the app. If the repo has multiple independent entry points that each reach an LLM/agent/tool, give each its own workflow name describing what THAT one does.
- Calling `init()` again with the same configuration is idempotent; calling it with conflicting configuration raises a configuration error until the current SDK generation is shut down. Never add a second `init()` to switch projects inside one running process. Almost every independent entry point you find stays on the same project and is distinguished by its own workflow root. Use a secondary client only when telemetry genuinely belongs to a different Neatlogs project (for example, explicit multi-tenant routing), and confirm that ownership decision with the user rather than inferring it from code structure.
- Capture each LLM/framework call using the mechanism Step 3's reference says to use for that specific provider or framework — do not wrap something the guide says to instrument a different way, and never apply two mechanisms to the same call (e.g. `wrap()` a client AND also list it in `instrumentations=[...]`).
- `wrap()`/`instrumentations=[...]`/framework integrations only capture library calls. Add a manual `@neatlogs.span(kind="WORKFLOW")` / `trace()` around a feature entry point only when you need to GROUP several of those calls under one named trace — not as an alternative way to capture a single call.

## Step 5: Verify instrumentation and ingestion

Use the language guide to run the installed SDK's `doctor --local` and `doctor --probe` commands with the SDK project key and regional ingest endpoint. These are SDK commands, not subcommands of `neatlogs-cli`. Do not guess the Python, TypeScript, or Go invocation. For HTTP/OTLP-only integrations, follow their guide's verification path instead.

Do not run the application yourself. Ask the user to run an instrumented entry point and provide its trace ID or result. A synthetic Doctor probe verifies the telemetry pipeline; report it separately from verification of the user's actual application trace. Do not claim application instrumentation passed based only on a synthetic probe. With only the SDK project key, use Doctor readback and mark CLI readback "waiting on a human".

## Step 6: Optional public API CLI readback

Install `neatlogs-cli` using `npm install --global neatlogs-cli` and check `neatlogs --version` (Node.js 22 or 24). The SDK key must remain available to the application, but it must not override CLI authentication.

Use the dashboard-specific profile `setup-https---app-neatlogs-com` consistently for login and every read. Before signing in, inspect `neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com profile list`. Reuse this name only if it is unused or already belongs to this exact dashboard origin; otherwise choose an unused name and replace it in every command below. Login creates the profile when needed. Do not rebind an authenticated profile from another dashboard or rely on the default/active profile.

For human OAuth, the following POSIX-shell commands exclude SDK/environment credentials only from each CLI process; they do not unset the application's key. In other shells, launch the CLI in an environment without those variables. A CLI version exposing `--credential-source profile` in `--help` can use that option instead of excluding the two credential variables.

env -u NEATLOGS_API_KEY -u NEATLOGS_TOKEN -u NEATLOGS_PROJECT_ID neatlogs --host https://app.neatlogs.com --profile setup-https---app-neatlogs-com projects list
